# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–26 (Complete – Updated 187)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of seventh year, transitioning to autumn** (Chapter 26). John Sedley **deceased**—died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside his wife. Major Dobbin returned to England, reunited with Amelia. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established at Russell Square with grandfather.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 24 opened "winter of sixth year"; Chapter 25 opened "spring of seventh year"; Chapter 26 opens "summer of seventh year" and extends into autumn.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton (churchyard).

## The Duel and Its Resolution (Chapter 23–24)
**Duel Outcome**: Secret rencontre between Rawdon and Steyne; outcome buried "in profoundest oblivion" by agreement but story spread rapidly. Scandal suppressed from newspapers by Wagg acting on Wenham's hint.

**Rawdon's Refusal of Reconciliation**: Refused Pitt's reconciliation message. Rebecca concealed money ten years; Rawdon declared he would never see her again, "If she's not guilty, Pitt, she's as bad as guilty."

**Rawdon's Acceptance of Governorship**: Initially resisted Steyne's gift. Persuaded by Pitt and especially Macmurdo's argument that accepting position would spite Steyne by making him instrument of Rawdon's prosperity.

## Rebecca's Fate (Chapter 24)
Bailiffs seized Curzon Street property. Rawdon made Rebecca "tolerable annuity." Her whereabouts unknown; "Who cared!"

## Rawdon's Transformation (Chapter 24)
Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand per year. Complete moral transformation: maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education, compensates those wronged.

## Georgy Osborne (Chapter 24–26)
**Establishment**: "Fairly established in his grandfather's mansion in Russell Square," heir apparent to splendours. Mr. Osborne "as proud of him as ever" of elder George.

**Character and Dominance**: Scarcely eleven years old. Superior education made him "much better gentleman" than grandfather; boy's "quick brain" revealed grandfather "a dullard." Boy began commanding grandfather, who "was afraid of Georgy." Dressed daily for dinner as "West End swell" with straps, boots, gilt spurs, gold-headed whip. One domestic attended him. After breakfast, read Morning Post "like a grown-up man." Made house lively by activity, imperiousness, scolding, good-nature.

**School and Academics**: Day boy at Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Hart Street, Bloomsbury). Veal is domestic Chaplain to Earl of Bareacres. Marked aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French. Schoolboys call Veal "Longtail"—name Georgy gave him.

**Friendships**: Young Todd of Coram Street was Georgy's great friend. Both attended principal theatres, knew actors' names. **Mrs. Todd's plan (rumor)**: Privately wondered if Georgy and her daughter Rosa Jemima "might happen."

**Admiration for Dobbin (Chapter 25)**: "Georgy never tired of his praises" to mother. Told Amelia Dobbin "knows such lots of things" and "reads Latin like English." Heard Colonel Buckler say Dobbin "was one of the bravest officers in the army." Separated easily from Amelia; she yearned "every hour of the day."

**Miniature Portrait**: Commissioned miniature of himself from own money; old Osborne doubled the sovereigns paid. Amelia hung it beside George's over her bed. Visits mother in Gillespie Street once or twice weekly, "bullied the servants and his relations there, just as he did in Russell Square."

**Grandfather's Reconciliation**: Old Osborne's attitude toward Dobbin shifted markedly. Initially scornful of Dobbin, Osborne heard from various society members and Sir William Dobbin of Major's distinguished reputation, learning, valor. Dobbin's name appeared in guest lists of nobility, having "prodigious effect upon the old aristocrat of Russell Square."

## John Sedley's Final Illness and Death (Chapter 26)

**Onset and Nursing**: Shortly after Mrs. Sedley's death and Jos's return, old man "was about to go seek for his wife in the dark land." Old Sedley "clung to his daughter during this sickness...scarcely any other hand" gave him broths and medicines. "To tend him became almost the sole business of her life." Her bed placed close to his chamber door; she was alert to "the slightest noise or disturbance from the couch of the querulous invalid."

**Reconciliation with Amelia**: Old man "lay awake many an hour, silent and without stirring, unwilling to awaken his kind and vigilant nurse." In his final illness, "touched by her love and goodness, the old man forgot all his grief against her, and wrongs which he and his wife had many a long night debated." He had charged her with giving up everything for her boy, carelessness of parents in old age and misfortune, impious grief over George's death. One night, "the broken old man made his confession": "Oh, Emmy, I've been thinking we were very unkind and unjust to you." She knelt and prayed by his bedside as he held her hand.

**Death**: John Sedley died peacefully in sleep. **Date of death (fact)**: "One morning and sunrise when all the world got up and set about its various works and pleasures, with the exception of old John Sedley, who was not to fight with fortune, or to hope or scheme any more." Buried at Brompton churchyard by the side of his wife. Major Dobbin, Jos, and Georgy followed remains to grave in black cloth coach. Jos came from Star and Garter at Richmond, "whither he retreated after the deplorable event...did not care to remain in the house." Amelia "stayed and did her duty as usual...bowed down by no especial grief, and rather solemn than sorrowful." She prayed her own end might be as calm and painless, thought with trust and reverence of her father's words during illness, "indicative of his faith, his resignation, and his future hope."

## Major Dobbin's Return and Reconciliation with Old Osborne (Chapter 24–26)

**Illness in Madras**: Obtained leave, travelled "night and day" to Madras "in a high fever." Lay "tossing in his fever...raving about Amelia." Made testament, left property "to those whom he most desired to benefit." Wore "little brown hair-chain...from Amelia's maid at Brussels...when the young widow's hair was cut off, during the fever which prostrated her after the death of George Osborne."

**Passage and Journey**: After St. Helena, displayed "gaiety and strength." Became "impatient and ill-humoured" within ten days' sail; recovered when breeze sprang up. "Good God, how his heart beat as the two friendly spires of Southampton came in sight." Travelled rapidly to London; at Slaughters' Inn, inquired about "Captain Osborne's widow." Chose "smartest...civil costume."

**Reunion with Clapps**: Called on Clapps in Brompton; greeted by Miss Mary Polly Clapp. **Reverend Binny's Marriage**: Learned Binny married Miss Grits (grocer's daughter, five thousand pound fortune). Dobbin's "head was swimming with felicity"—"no longer a rival to fear."

**Meeting with Amelia**: Old Sedley sat on bench. Amelia feared something happened to Georgy; sight of messenger's happy face dissipated fear. Dobbin's "lean figure and long shadow stalking across the grass" caused her to start, blush, cry. She came "running towards him, her hands before her." "She wasn't changed. She was a little pale, a little stouter in figure. Her eyes were the same, the kind trustful eyes. There were scarce three lines of silver in her soft brown hair." He took "the two little hands between his two and held them there. He was speechless for a moment."

**Declaration and Refusal**: Dobbin declared: "Amelia, Amelia...I did buy it for you. I loved you then as I do now...I think there is no hour in the day has passed for twelve years that I haven't thought of you." Amelia steadfastly refused: "George is my husband, here and in heaven. How could I love any other but him?...You are everything to me and my boy...our dearest, truest, kindest friend and protector." Voice broke; she hid face on his shoulder. Told Polly "never, never" to speak of remarriage; could not remarry after such an angel. "Not displeased by Dobbin's attachment; would give him 'friendly regard, which so much excellence and fidelity merited.'"

**Discovery of Dobbin's Support**: During Sedley's illness, old Osborne, "a keen man of business, looking into the Major's accounts with his ward and the boy's mother," discovered "it was out of William Dobbin's own pocket that a part of the fund had been supplied upon which the poor widow and the child had subsisted." When pressed, Dobbin "blushed and stammered a good deal and finally confessed": "The marriage...was very much my doing. I thought my poor friend had gone so far that retreat from his engagement would have been dishonour to him and death to Mrs. Osborne, and I could do no less, when she was left without resources, than give what money I could spare to maintain her."

**Old Osborne's Reaction and Reconciliation**: Osborne "looked hard at him and turning very red." Said: "Major D....you did me a great injury; but give me leave to tell you, sir, you are an honest feller. There's my hand, sir, though I little thought that my flesh and blood was living on you--" The pair "shook hands, with great confusion on Major Dobbin's part, thus found out in his act of charitable hypocrisy."

**Softening of Osborne**: Dobbin "strove to soften the old man and reconcile him towards his son's memory." Said: "He was such a noble fellow...all of us loved him, and would have done anything for him...I, as a young man in those days, was flattered beyond measure by his preference for me...I never saw his equal for pluck and daring and all the qualities of a soldier." Dobbin told "as many stories as he could remember regarding the gallantry and achievements of his son," adding "And Georgy is so like him." Dobbin dined with Osborne during Sedley's sickness; they discussed departed hero. "His mood was at any rate better and more charitable than that in which he had been disposed until now to regard the poor fellow; and the Christian heart of the kind Major was pleased at these symptoms of returning peace and good-will." On second evening, "old Osborne called Dobbin William, just as he used to do at the time when Dobbin and George were boys together, and the honest gentleman was pleased by that mark of reconciliation."

**Osborne's Public Defense**: At breakfast, when Miss Osborne "with the asperity of her age and character, ventured to make some remark reflecting slightingly upon the Major's appearance or behaviour," master of house interrupted: "You'd have been glad enough to git him for yourself, Miss O. But them grapes are sour. Ha! ha! Major William is a fine feller."

## Amelia's New Life and Household (Chapter 25–26)

**Separation from Mary Clapp**: Mary's sorrow at departure "such as I shall not attempt to depict." When barouche came, "she fainted in the arms of her friend." Amelia "endowed Mary with every article of furniture that the house contained, only taking away her pictures...and her piano." **Plan (rumor)**: "Poor Mary...was placed under the medical treatment of the young fellow from the surgery, under whose care she rallied."

**New Household**: Butler was Jos's valet; Emmy supplied maid "grown on Sir William Dobbin's suburban estate"; maid's "kindness and humility disarmed Mrs. Osborne...who did not in the least know how to use one." Maid useful tending old Mr. Sedley.

**Social Acceptance (Chapter 25)**: "Numbers of people came to see Mrs. Osborne." Lady Dobbin and daughters waited upon her. Miss Osborne came in grand chariot. Jos "reported to be immensely rich." Emmy had visiting-book, drove regularly in carriage. "Buttony boy" sprang up and down with visiting-cards. Voted "rather a pleasing young person--not much in her, but pleasing."

**Young Indian Officers**: Young Indian dandies on furlough admired Mrs. Osborne, paid morning visits. Swankey of Body Guard discovered by Dobbin "tete-a-tete with Amelia, and describing the sport of pig-sticking to her with great humour and eloquence."

**Jos at Court**: After attending Drawing-room in full court suit, became "such a tremendous Tory and pillar of the State" he insisted Amelia attend Drawing-room. "He somehow had worked himself up to believe that he was implicated in the maintenance of the public welfare."

## Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 23–24)
Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand per year. Complete moral transformation: maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education, compensates those wronged. Separated from Rebecca permanently after duel.
